cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
Today we look inside the nucleus and connect its structure with energy.
Start with three symbols.
Z is the number of protons, N is the number of neutrons, and A is the total
number of nucleons.
Therefore A equals Z plus N.
For iron fifty six, Z is twenty six.
Subtract twenty six from fifty six and you get thirty neutrons.
A neutral atom also has twenty six electrons, but those electrons are not
included in the nuclear mass number.
Isotopes have the same proton number and different neutron numbers.
Their chemistry can be similar because they belong to the same element, while
their nuclear properties can differ.
Now a units trap.
Mass number fifty six does not mean the actual atomic mass is exactly fifty
six
unified atomic mass units.
A is a count.
The unit u is defined as one twelfth of the mass of a neutral carbon twelve
atom in its ground state at rest.
Notice the word atom, not bare nucleus.
Atomic mass tables generally include the electrons of neutral atoms.
Nuclear mass tables do not.
We will keep that distinction when calculating binding energy.
Pause and test the notation: if an isotope has A equal to forty and Z equal to
twenty, how many neutrons are inside?
Twenty.
Begin each nuclear question by counting particles and identifying whether the
stated mass belongs to a nucleus or an atom.
That small check saves a surprising number of mistakes.
A nucleus is incredibly small compared with an atom.
A useful empirical estimate for its radius is R zero times A to the one third
power.
Use R zero approximately one point two femtometers for our examples.
A femtometer is ten to the minus fifteen meters.
The one third power means a cube root.
Why that particular dependence?
Nuclear matter has approximately the same density across many nuclei.
Adding nucleons roughly adds volume.
If volume grows in proportion to A and a sphere's volume grows as radius
cubed,
radius must grow as the cube root of A.
Real nuclei have diffuse boundaries and can be nonspherical, so this is an
average model rather than an exact ruler for every isotope.
Take A equal to one hundred twenty five.
The cube root is five, giving radius about six femtometers.
Now compare nuclei with mass numbers sixty four and two hundred sixteen.
Their cube roots are four and six.
The radius ratio is six over four, or one point five.
The mass number ratio is larger, three point three seven five.
Their volumes have approximately that same larger ratio, because volume
depends
on radius cubed.
Think before answering a ratio question: does it ask for radius, volume, or
density?
They are not interchangeable.
In the simple spherical model, mass and volume both scale with A, so A cancels
from the density expression.
Nearly constant nuclear density follows from the same scaling assumption; it
is
not an independent numerical coincidence.
Here comes the central energy idea.
A bound nucleus has a lower rest mass than its separated protons and neutrons.
That difference is called the mass defect.
Energy is released when the bound state forms, and energy must be supplied to
separate it completely.
This does not violate conservation: total mass energy, including released
radiation and kinetic energy, is conserved.
If you use bare nuclear masses, subtract the nuclear mass from the sum of bare
proton and neutron masses.
If you use neutral atomic masses instead, use hydrogen atom mass for each
proton contribution.
The electron rest masses then cancel to excellent approximation, while small
electronic binding corrections are neglected at this nuclear scale.
Let's calculate for deuterium, containing one proton and one neutron.
Use hydrogen atom mass one point zero zero seven eight two five u, neutron
mass
one point zero zero eight six six five u, and deuterium atomic mass two point
zero one four one zero two u.
Add the first two and subtract the third.
The defect is zero point zero zero two three eight eight u.
Multiply by nine hundred thirty one point five mega electron volts per u.
The binding energy is approximately two point two two four mega electron
volts.
For binding energy per nucleon, divide by A equal to two, giving about one
point one one two mega electron volts.
Do not mix a bare proton mass with a neutral deuterium atomic mass.
Consistent mass bookkeeping comes before the multiplication.
Now plot binding energy per nucleon against mass number.
For very light nuclei the values are relatively small, with important
irregularities between neighboring nuclei.
The broad curve rises toward a peak near the iron and nickel region, around
eight point eight mega electron volts per nucleon, and then declines gradually
for very heavy nuclei.
This graph gives an energy direction, not a universal rule that every
imaginable reaction must occur.
Light nuclei can release energy by combining into products with greater total
binding.
Some heavy nuclei can release energy by splitting into more tightly bound
products.
Here is the reason: greater binding means a lower combined rest mass for the
same conserved particles, with the difference available as released energy.
Be careful with the word per.
To calculate the exact energy of a reaction, compare total binding energies or
consistent total rest masses of all reactants and products.
A single per nucleon number cannot replace that bookkeeping.
If a nucleus with A equal to fifty has binding energy per nucleon eight mega
electron volts, its total binding energy is four hundred mega electron volts.
Pause before using that total as reaction energy.
It is not automatically the energy released in any particular change.
The products also carry binding energy.
Likewise, a large binding energy per nucleon does not by itself prove that
every possible radioactive decay is forbidden.
Charge, nucleon balance, available final states, and the complete energy
comparison matter.
Read the curve as a useful trend, then calculate the stated reaction.
Let's bring the energy story together.
Fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into lighter products.
One possible illustrative channel is uranium two hundred thirty five plus a
neutron forming barium one hundred forty one, krypton ninety two, and three
neutrons.
Count the mass numbers: two hundred thirty six on the left, and one hundred
forty one plus ninety two plus three on the right.
Charge numbers also balance: ninety two equals fifty six plus thirty six.
Real fission has many product channels, so this example is not the only
outcome.
Energy release is typically of order two hundred mega electron volts per
fission, depending on the complete channel and energy accounting.
Fusion combines light nuclei.
An illustrative reaction is deuterium plus tritium forming helium four and a
neutron.
Mass number is five on both sides, and charge number is two on both sides.
This reaction releases about seventeen point six mega electron volts.
The positive nuclei repel electrically, so merely having an energy favorable
product does not remove the approach barrier; quantum tunneling also matters.
Our focus is conceptual nuclear energy, not engineering a device.
For a numerical example, if the total initial rest mass exceeds the final
total
by zero point zero one eight nine u, Q is that difference times nine hundred
thirty one point five, approximately seventeen point six mega electron volts.
A positive Q means energy is released.
A negative Q means energy must be supplied, with additional kinematic
conditions potentially relevant.
Balance particles first, use one consistent mass convention, and only then
evaluate the energy difference.
